title: Introduction to Economics
summary: Understand scarcity, supply and demand, elasticity, market failure, GDP, inflation, unemployment and trade, with calculations you can check.
audience: Secondary students, first-year university students and curious readers

body.p: Economics studies how people, firms and governments choose when resources are limited. Wants are unlimited, but time, money, land, labour and equipment are scarce. Scarcity forces choice, and every choice has a cost. The opportunity cost of a choice is the value of the next best alternative you give up. It is not the sum of everything you did not choose.

Example: a student has one free evening. She can work a shift for 8,000 or study for a test. If she studies, her opportunity cost is the 8,000 she could have earned. For a government, building a hospital with a fixed budget may mean one fewer school.

A production possibility frontier (PPF) shows the maximum combinations of two goods an economy can produce with all its resources. A point on the curve is efficient. A point inside it means resources are unused or wasted, for example during high unemployment. A point outside is not possible now but may be reached through growth, such as new technology or more skilled workers.

list: Positive statements can be tested with data: Unemployment fell from 9% to 8%.
Normative statements are opinions about what should be: The government should raise the minimum wage.
Economists use positive analysis to describe the world and normative judgement to decide policy.

lessons.title: Demand, supply and the market price

body.p: Demand is the quantity buyers are willing and able to buy at each price. The law of demand says that, other things equal, a higher price means a lower quantity demanded. Supply is the quantity sellers are willing to offer at each price. A higher price usually means a higher quantity supplied because production becomes more profitable.

The market clears where quantity demanded equals quantity supplied. Suppose demand is Qd = 100 - 2P and supply is Qs = 20 + 2P. Set them equal: 100 - 2P = 20 + 2P, so 80 = 4P and P = 20. At that price Qd = 100 - 40 = 60 and Qs = 20 + 40 = 60. The equilibrium price is 20 and the quantity is 60.

If the price is held at 15, Qd = 100 - 30 = 70 and Qs = 20 + 30 = 50. Demand exceeds supply by 20, so there is a shortage. Prices tend to rise until the market clears. If the price were 25, Qd = 50 and Qs = 70, a surplus of 20, and prices tend to fall.

list: A change in the good's own price causes a movement along the curve.
A change in income, tastes, the price of related goods, population or expectations shifts the demand curve.
A change in costs, technology, taxes or weather shifts the supply curve.

body.tip: When a question asks what happens after a change, first say which curve shifts, then which direction, then what happens to the equilibrium price and quantity.

body.p: Elasticity measures how strongly quantity responds to a change in something else. Price elasticity of demand (PED) is the percentage change in quantity demanded divided by the percentage change in price.

Example: a shop raises the price of a juice from 100 to 110, a 10% rise. Weekly sales fall from 200 to 170, a fall of 15%. PED = -15 / 10 = -1.5. We usually ignore the minus sign and say the PED is 1.5. A value above 1 means demand is elastic: buyers react strongly. Below 1 means inelastic: buyers react weakly. Exactly 1 is unit elastic.

list: If demand is elastic, raising the price lowers total revenue, because the fall in sales outweighs the higher price. Here revenue was 100 x 200 = 20,000 and becomes 110 x 170 = 18,700.
If demand is inelastic, raising the price raises revenue.
Governments tax goods with inelastic demand, such as fuel and tobacco, to raise revenue.
Many close substitutes are available.
The good is a luxury rather than a necessity.
The good takes a large share of the buyer's income.
Buyers have a long time to adjust.

body.p: Markets usually allocate resources well, but not always. Market failure occurs when the free market gives an outcome that is not the best for society.

list: Externalities: costs or benefits that fall on third parties, such as pollution (negative) or vaccination (positive).
Public goods: goods like street lighting that no one can be excluded from and that one person's use does not reduce, so private firms under-supply them.
Information problems: buyers cannot judge quality, such as in used cars or medicines.
Monopoly power: one seller can restrict output and raise prices.
Taxes on harmful goods to make users pay the full cost.
Subsidies for goods with positive externalities such as education or clean energy.
Regulation and standards, such as emission limits or food safety rules.
Provision of public goods directly or through public funding.

body.p: Government action also has costs. It can be badly designed, slow, or captured by special interests. Government failure occurs when intervention makes the outcome worse. Good policy compares the benefits of a fix with its costs.
Macroeconomics looks at the whole economy. Gross domestic product (GDP) is the value of final goods and services produced in a country in a period, usually a year.

GDP = C + I + G + (X - M), where C is household consumption, I is investment by firms, G is government spending, X is exports and M is imports. If C = 600, I = 200, G = 150, X = 100 and M = 120 (all in billions), then net exports are 100 - 120 = -20 and GDP = 600 + 200 + 150 - 20 = 930. Real GDP removes the effect of price changes so that growth reflects real output.

Inflation is a sustained rise in the general price level, measured by a price index such as the consumer price index (CPI). If the CPI rises from 120 to 126, inflation is (126 - 120) / 120 = 5%. If your wage rises 8% when prices rise 5%, your real wage rises by about 2.9%, because 1.08 / 1.05 = 1.029. If your wage rises less than inflation, your purchasing power falls.

The unemployment rate is the number of unemployed people divided by the labour force (employed plus unemployed). With 92 employed and 8 unemployed, the rate is 8 / 100 = 8%. Causes include a lack of demand, a mismatch of skills and the structure of industries changing.

Governments and central banks use policy to steer the economy. Fiscal policy is government taxation and spending. Lower taxes or higher spending can boost demand in a downturn, but borrowing to pay for it adds to public debt. Monetary policy is run by the central bank, mainly through the interest rate. Raising the rate makes borrowing costlier and tends to slow inflation, while cutting it encourages spending and investment.
An exchange rate is the price of one currency in another. If a weaker local currency makes imports dearer, inflation can rise, but exporters may gain because their goods become cheaper abroad.

Comparative advantage says countries gain from trade when each specialises in what it produces at the lowest opportunity cost, even if one country is better at everything. Trade gives choice and lower prices, but some industries and workers lose out when imports compete, and policy may be needed to help them adjust. Tariffs, quotas and subsidies are common trade barriers.

body.tip: In an exam, do not only say that something is good or bad. Name who gains, who loses, and how big the effect is likely to be.

options: The money spent on a purchase
The value of the next best alternative given up
The total of all alternatives not chosen
The price of the cheapest option
The government should raise the minimum wage
